index.html.intro.p: brings research, lived experience and African voices together to examine the systems shaping the continent, and to explore practical pathways towards African agency, excellence and renewal.

index.html.latest.p: Why African education often prepares young people to leave local opportunities rather than transform them, and what an education designed from African realities would do instead.

index.html.why.p: Its challenge is that much of its intelligence has not been sufficiently recognised, refined, institutionalised, financed and transformed into collective power. This platform moves beyond describing Africa's problems: it asks how they were produced, what sustains them, what knowledge has been neglected, and what practical alternatives can be built.
index.html.sci.h2: >This is not the past. This is interrupted science.
index.html.sci.p: The clay pot is not a symbol of poverty; it is an off-grid thermodynamic device, refined through generations of empirical experimentation. Using AI speculative imaging, we project what African sciences should look like today, had their development never been violently interrupted.
index.html.sci.cap1: <figcaption>"Subsistence craft": the colonial framing of African knowledge.</figcaption>
index.html.sci.cap2: <figcaption>Thermodynamics, computation, engineering: scientific archives awaiting restoration.</figcaption>
index.html.sci.quote: >What was interrupted can be restored. What was deferred can be recovered.
index.html.pics.cap1: <figcaption>The Clay Pot Evolution: traditional wisdom, modern science.</figcaption>

index.html.pics.cap3: <figcaption>From Great Zimbabwe to the smart city: built by Africa, for Africa.</figcaption>

index.html.theme4.p: Why Africa imports expertise and how local capability can be strengthened.

index.html.question.q2: What is one thing African education trains us to leave behind?

index.html.voices.p:
Scholars, artisans, students, entrepreneurs, elders, policymakers
      and the diaspora. Each month this platform features one African voice and the knowledge they
      carry. If that is you, or someone you know, tell us.
index.html.written.p:
Articles, research summaries, reading lists and downloadable briefs
      sit alongside the episodes. This is what separates the platform from commentary: every claim
      can be traced to a source.
index.html.join.h2: >Africa's future cannot be imagined by one voice
index.html.join.p: Bring your research, experience, question or story into the conversation.
index.html.founder.alt: alt="Dr Oluwakemi Damola Adejumo-Ayibiowu, wearing an indigo and gold adire-print dress"
index.html.founder.p: Dr Damola is a development economist, Afrocentric scholar, AI generalist, public policy strategist and gospel music artist with over 25 years of experience across government, academia and international consultancy. Through Rethinking Africa she brings scholarship out of restricted academic spaces and into public conversation.
index.html.founder.for: For scholars, students, policymakers, professionals, creators, community leaders, members of the diaspora, and everyone committed to Africa's intellectual and developmental renewal.
index.html.sub.p: Be among the first thousand members of a movement to recover African intelligence and agency. Discover African-centred perspectives grounded in research, watch conversations with scholars and practitioners, and receive new episodes, articles and event invitations, beginning with the free 7 Days of Rethinking series.

quiz.html.q1: "Growing up, were you taught that knowledge from Europe or America was better than knowledge from Africa?"
quiz.html.q1.a2: "Nobody said it, but I felt it"
quiz.html.q1.a4: "I never thought about it this way"
quiz.html.q1.text: "Six hundred years ago, Timbuktu in Mali was a city of scholars. Families kept libraries in their homes. Hundreds of thousands of handwritten books on medicine, astronomy, mathematics and law. Students came from far away to study there. It was a university city before many European ones existed."
quiz.html.q1.why: "In 1591 an invading army destroyed the scholarly community and its leading scholars were killed or taken away. Later, under French colonial rule, the schools that replaced it taught a different story, and many manuscripts were carried off to Europe. Families hid what was left in boxes and buried them. The books survived. The universities did not."
quiz.html.q2: "Did your education bring you closer to your own community, or take you further away from it?"
quiz.html.q2.text: "Before colonial schooling, most African children learned a trade, a craft or a body of knowledge from the people around them. Farming, weaving, building, healing, trading. Learning happened inside the community and stayed there."
quiz.html.q2.why: "Colonial schools were built for a stated purpose: to produce clerks and messengers who could serve an administration, not builders, inventors or owners. Children were taught in a foreign language, about foreign places, and were punished for speaking their own. When independence came, the flags changed. In many countries the syllabus did not. If school made you feel your home had nothing to teach you, that was the design working, not you failing."
quiz.html.q3: "You see a clay water pot in a village. What do you think?"
quiz.html.q3.a2: "Poverty, honestly. That is what I was taught"
quiz.html.q3.a4: "I use one. I never thought about it"
quiz.html.q3.text: "A clay pot keeps water cold in extreme heat with no electricity at all. Water passes slowly through the clay wall, and as it evaporates on the outside it pulls heat away from the water inside. It is real science, worked out over generations by testing which clay, which thickness, which shape kept water coldest."
quiz.html.q3.why: "Nobody funded it. No laboratory studied it, no company improved it, no patent protected it, no university taught it. It was called craft instead of science, so it stayed the same size for centuries. Today engineers in Europe and the Gulf use exactly this cooling principle in modern buildings, and it is described as an innovation."
quiz.html.q4: "An elder starts explaining traditional knowledge to you. What is your first instinct?"
quiz.html.q4.a2: "Ask how we could test and prove it"
quiz.html.q4.a4: "Introduce them to someone who could use it"
quiz.html.q4.text: "Every computer and phone in the world runs on binary: everything reduced to two states, on or off, 1 or 0, and then combined to build anything. The Ifa system of the Yoruba works on exactly the same principle. Each mark is one of two states. Four marks make one figure. Sixteen figures combine into 256 outcomes, each attached to a body of memorised verses. It is a binary information system, held in trained human memory, over a thousand years old."
quiz.html.q4.why: "It was labelled superstition. Missionaries and colonial officials discouraged it, converts were told to abandon it, and it was never allowed into a single university mathematics department. So the same logic that became the computer in one part of the world was called witchcraft in another. Nobody in Africa was invited to the meeting where binary became a machine."
quiz.html.q5: "What worries you most about Africa today?"
quiz.html.q5.a3: "Identity, and the stories told about us"
quiz.html.q5.text: "Great Zimbabwe is a city of stone walls up to eleven metres high, built without any cement. The stones are cut so precisely that they hold each other in place, and have done for about eight hundred years. It was the centre of a wealthy trading kingdom connected to the Indian Ocean."
quiz.html.q5.why: "When Europeans found it, they refused to believe Africans had built it. Colonial authorities pushed the story that foreigners must have done it. Treasure hunters dug through the site for gold and threw away the very layers of soil that held the proof, destroying the evidence. Later archaeologists who said plainly that Africans built it were pressured to stay quiet. The building was African. So was the truth. Both were buried."
quiz.html.q6: "Do you live in Africa, or outside it?"
quiz.html.q6.text: "The money Africans abroad send home every year is now larger than all the foreign aid the continent receives. It arrives with no conditions, no consultants and no forms. It pays school fees, builds houses, buries parents and starts businesses."
quiz.html.q6.why: "Nothing stopped this one, and that is the point. It is the clearest proof that Africans already fund Africa. What is missing is not money or willingness. It is the institutions that would turn millions of small private acts into schools, factories and companies that outlive the person who paid for them."
quiz.html.q7: "Finish this sentence. Africa's future will be built mainly by..."
quiz.html.q7.text: "Notice the pattern in everything you just read. None of it failed. None of it was disproved. Each one was interrupted: invaded, defunded, renamed, ridiculed or buried. And in every case the knowledge itself survived, in a pot, in a memory, in a wall, in a hidden box."
quiz.html.q7.why: "That is the whole argument of this platform. Africa is not empty of intelligence. Its intelligence was never recognised, protected, funded or passed on properly. That is not a tragedy you inherit. It is unfinished work, and unfinished work can be continued by whoever decides to pick it up."
quiz.html.p.KR.name: "The Knowledge Recoverer"
quiz.html.p.KR.desc: "You feel the loss of what is disappearing. Your instinct is to find it, write it down and keep it, before the last person who remembers is gone."
quiz.html.p.KR.strength: "Your strength is saving memory before it closes."
quiz.html.p.KR.q: "What did your grandparents know that your generation did not learn?"
quiz.html.p.BB.name: "The Bridge Builder"
quiz.html.p.BB.desc: "You live between two worlds, and that is not confusion, it is an advantage. Your instinct is to connect people, money and ideas that would otherwise never meet."
quiz.html.p.BB.strength: "Your strength is standing in two places at once."
quiz.html.p.BB.q: "Who do you know on each side who has never met the other?"
quiz.html.p.SR.name: "The System Reformer"
quiz.html.p.SR.desc: "You know that good intentions are not enough, because systems decide what happens long before individuals do. Your instinct is rules, standards and institutions that work."
quiz.html.p.SR.strength: "Your strength is building what outlasts you."
quiz.html.p.SR.q: "Which broken system near you was designed by someone who never had to live inside it?"
quiz.html.p.ST.name: "The Story Restorer"
quiz.html.p.ST.desc: "You understand that people slowly become the story told about them. Your instinct is words, images and culture that give people back their confidence."
quiz.html.p.ST.strength: "Your strength is changing what people believe they are allowed to want."
quiz.html.p.ST.q: "Whose story about Africa are you still repeating without checking?"
quiz.html.p.FM.name: "The Future Maker"
quiz.html.p.FM.desc: "Recovering the past is not enough for you. You want to build things that have never existed anywhere, starting from African ground."
quiz.html.p.FM.strength: "Your strength is refusing the options you were given."
quiz.html.p.FM.q: "What would you build if you stopped waiting for permission?"
